A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tversky Neural Networks work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reordering and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original XOR training experiments, MNIST and NABirds classification results, PTB language-modeling results and learned-feature visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and evaluation results and additionally reports held-out PTB test perplexities, token-semantic analyses and prototype evolution.

M1.justification: Equation 5 revises the specified substractmatch operator: v2 adds the ignorematch contribution for features exclusive to A to the excess shared-feature contribution, whereas v1 includes only the latter. This changes the operator as written; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed. The principal neural modules and feature-sharing mechanism remain.

E1.justification: XOR, MNIST, NABirds and PTB remain the principal coverage. v2 adds qualitative retrieval scenarios using algebraically specified semantic fields, including token morphology, grammatical categories and word senses, plus MNIST instance retrieval by common and distinctive features (Table 3 and Appendices E–F).

E2.justification: The PTB validation comparisons in Tables 8–11 drop the tversky-all-2layers variant, retaining GPT-2, tversky-head and tversky-all-1layer. The ResNet-50 and MNISTNet/VisualMNISTNet baselines remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 explicitly selects Tversky models using PTB validation results and evaluates the selected models and baselines on the held-out test split; v1's main table reports validation perplexities. The reported configuration grid also contracts, removing two-layer variants and the 256-, 512- and 50,257-feature configurations. These materially change the reported evaluation design, while the principal training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretability analyses with token-semantic case studies, prototype evolution across training epochs and ranked MNIST instances for feature-set expressions. It removes v1's MNIST feature-count/normalization sensitivity analysis and narrows the PTB architecture and feature-size sweeps. The XOR sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The XOR nine-seed specification and mean/standard-error reporting in Tables 4–7 are unchanged. Removing the checklist deletes v1's explicit disclosure that GPT-2 and ResNet-50 results omit error bars because of computational cost. Neither version supplies uncertainty estimates for those comparisons, and no increase in repetitions is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds test perplexities rather than improving the same validation measurements. For scratch training with tied prototypes, v1 Table 2 reports baseline/Tversky validation PPL of 136.04/125.86, while v2 Table 1 reports test PPL of 112.81/103.99. Retained appendix validation rows are numerically unchanged, but numerous configurations disappear. Semantic-field and prototype-evolution findings are added; the main vision accuracies and XOR statistics remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 5 substantively corrects the formal set-difference definition by including Equation 4's contribution for features absent from B. This is not equivalent notation. v2 also states the feature-sum score used for semantic-field ranking, while retaining the XOR and binary-addition constructions without new proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract revises the claimed PTB perplexity reduction from 7.5% to 7.8%, reflecting the newly reported test results. The central claims about differentiable Tversky similarity, interpretability, the 24.7% NABirds improvement and 34.8% parameter reduction remain. The introduction still quotes 7.5%.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits the vision evidence to demonstrating successful settings and acknowledges the absence of separate validation and extensive tuning. It develops interpretations of semantic fields as grammatical categories and distinct word senses. It also corrects v1's reversed attribution of tied versus untied PTB improvements, while retaining the principal salience, prototype and parameter-count interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the MNIST feature-bank size as 20 and documents semantic visualizations using the top 1,000 features, top 50 tokens and a force-directed layout. It removes the MNIST timing/GPU disclosure and the checklist's promise to release PyTorch implementations, experiment code and Makefiles. Existing qualitative-model training details are moved to Appendix F, not newly introduced.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning against geometric similarity and previous visualization approaches remain the same. Reference ordering and citation formatting change, but no new literature or materially revised novelty positioning is introduced.

P1.justification: v2 reverses the language-modeling and image-recognition experiment order, substantially restructures Section 3.4 around prototypes, salience and semantic fields, and moves detailed qualitative-model methods into Appendix F. Discussion material is consolidated, appendices are reorganized and the NeurIPS checklist is removed. These constitute substantial structural editing beyond added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds the semantic-field table and graph series, prototype-evolution panels and a ranked-instance digit illustration. It removes the feature-vector panel from Figure 2 and the MNIST sensitivity and timing plots, and compresses the PTB tables by removing configurations. Figures and tables are relocated within a different typographic and header layout.

improvement.justification: v2 improves mathematical specification through Equation 5, strengthens the language-model evidence with separate held-out test evaluation, and makes interpretability claims more concrete through semantic-field examples. These gains outweigh the reduced sensitivity coverage and removal of timing and code-release disclosures. The improvement remains limited by unchanged uncertainty reporting for the larger models and the acknowledged lack of separate validation in the vision experiments.
